utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So good morning, everybody. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radislav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Brdjanin, good morning to you. Can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Ann Sutherland, Julian Nicholls, assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Sutherland. Appearances for the Radislav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is John Ackerman. I am assisted by Aleksander Vujic, and one of our interns, Kelly Seratis [phoen] is with us this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Any preliminaries on your part?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Before we begin the cross-examination of Mr. Treanor, I seek to tender three exhibits. And they are -- two of the exhibits are in relation to P2656, which is the excerpt of Radovan Karadzic's speech at the Bosnian Assembly session held on the 11th, 14th, and 15th October 1991. And for completeness, we have the entire transcript of the assembly session. And I would seek to make that P2656.2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objection on your part, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So the document is so admitted. It will be given the Exhibit number P2656.2, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honours, we do have an English translation of Mr. Brdjanin's speech at that assembly, but not the entire assembly yet. So I would seek to tender this portion of the English translation at this time. I also wish to tender videotapes on CD-ROM of that assembly session. They have just come into -- the Prosecution has just received the transcript and the videotapes pursuant to a request that we made to the government. And I would seek to make the videotape P2656.3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the one sheet of paper that you had in your hand a couple of seconds ago relative to Mr. Brdjanin's speech in English, is that part of 2656.2?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. That will become the whole translation. But at this stage we only have Mr. Brdjanin's speech and obviously Mr. Karadzic's speech.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So the CD-ROMs will be -- how many of them? Just one?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Five.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So they are going to be P2656.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: .3. And then the five of them will be pooled together with no further number to distinguish them one from the other?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: May I ask if the CD itself contains interpretation in English or only in the original language?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It's just in the original language, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then you have the transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And then the transcripts will be P2656.2. The B/C/S transcript is P2656.2. And the English translation that I have at the moment of Mr. Brdjanin, and then the videotape will be .3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The final document, Your Honour, is a document that we seek to tender. It's -- it is relevant to issues in this case. It's a combat report dated the 16th of August, 1993. I've shown it to Mr. Ackerman. It was disclosed to him yesterday, and I showed him the signed document this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And this is going to be what? P --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: P2682, which is the next Prosecution exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I take it, Mr. Ackerman, that there was no objection to the transcripts, to the tendering the transcripts and no objection to the tendering of the CD video recordings?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the combat report?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'd like to reserve that until I have a chance to read it. I haven't received it yet. It was put in my locker last night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So it is being admitted with the usual caveat. All right?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, any preliminaries on your part?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Just kind of to follow-up on our last meeting, today I have provided Your Honours and the Prosecutor a schedule of witnesses beginning Monday, 20 October through the week of 12 January, or part of that week. We've already found that it has a problem or two that will have to be corrected. If you look at the week of 25 November, only one of those witnesses is going to be able to called that week, so that would move everything else ahead a ways. But that's my best effort at this point to give the Prosecution what they requested in terms of witness order. And we'll try our best to stick with this. We're hoping we can go faster than this document indicates through these witnesses, and we may be able to. So we have that. Secondly, I have also provided this morning an updated witness list that contains the names of three expert witnesses. One is a new witness who I was finally able to make arrangements with late last night. There is one or possibly two more that we're still in negotiations with. I think within the next couple of days we'll have the answer on both of those. In addition, I have supplied the Prosecution with -- and the Court -- with that updated list. And as Your Honours know, that's a moving target. It's going to be continually updated as we go along, some of it involving taking some of the people off of it. But we haven't yet gotten to that point. So I think that my report this morning is that we're making progress, Your Honour, from where we were last week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Before I put these in my personal folder, any of the names that appear on these two sheets of paper and obviously on the summaries supposedly confidential or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, these documents all need to be treated as confidential, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That needs to be made clear for everybody who is coming in possession.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I made that clear to the Registrar when I handed them to her this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But it wasn't made clear to us, so I'm making it clear myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Any time I provide those witness lists and updates, they will always contain some persons whose names should not be divulged to the public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's perfect. And I take it there is agreement at least from the information that I have from my staff, that there is agreement between you and the Prosecution that there will be a break starting from the 14th of November up to and inclusive of the 24th of November?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And I apologise for the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. confusion about that. I had -- when we had last discussed it, my impression was the Prosecution was asking me to move it ahead a week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, that's the impression I got.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I then informed your chief legal officer that that's what we would do. And then I got a call from Prosecution saying "we really didn't mean that. We want to take it back --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We discussed it amongst ourselves. We are prepared to accommodate you whichever way you like it. If you prefer these dates, you will have these dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: These dates are fine, Your Honour. I understand you want me to file some kind of a motion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please. And just for the record because --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We'll get that filed right away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The other matter. Mr. Cunningham has been asked by me to stay an extra day in Texas for the purpose of conducting an interview of one of the expert witnesses that I was talking about. So he will not arrive back in The Hague until tomorrow. He was scheduled to be here today. He will be here tomorrow. So the next witness following today's witness, I ask will not be called for direct examination until 9.00 Friday morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Tomorrow is Thursday, no?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. I suspect, Your Honour, that I will take all of today and most of tomorrow with Mr. Treanor in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wasn't anticipating the cross-examination of Mr. Treanor to finish today. I mean, that was not my anticipation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It will not finish today. And I may say one other thing about that -- well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So at worst, we might finish early tomorrow. That's the only difference. That all right with you, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, we have no objection to that, just with the suggestion that if we begin Friday morning rather than whatever time tomorrow, we may go slightly into Monday. I mean, that's -- we have no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We're fully aware of that Your Honour. We have understood for some time that that might be the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So anything else? No?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The only other thing I would request, Your Honour, is I will be conducting the examination from over there. And I would ask -- I gave you all a memo much earlier regarding some health issues. I'd ask that today at least I be permitted to be seated during the examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Have you received --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That memo was a month and a half ago maybe. Nothing new, nothing exciting. It just explained a health condition that attacks me every now and then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I remember. I remember. But I thought that was -- you were passed that stage, over that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I was hoping.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, let's not make of it an issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any time you need to have the sitting suspended, interrupted, or stopped, or adjourned, Mr. Ackerman, because of health reasons, let us know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm just asking I be permitted to question the witness from a seated position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, that has never been a problem in any case. Even if you need to have the sitting interrupted for a while, please let us know. So shall we bring in Mr. Treanor. Thank you. And the documents that you were tendering and the CDs, we don't have them as yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. The CDs we can provide after the break, and when the usher comes back, we'll give him the other documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, just before we begin, I have a very short errata sheet. The errata sheet is in relation to Section 5 to the addendum report, the implementation section. Usher, if they can go to the registry and if they can go to Mr. Ackerman, and then... Your Honour, once you have the document in front of you, you will see that it's in relation to Kotor Varos, and this was dealt with Mr. Treanor in his examination-in-chief in relation to the tables at the back of the report, and this simply clarifies paragraphs 171, 174, and 179 of the report where Kotor Varos was affected and also in relation to Prijedor within the table of the concurrent evidence and implementation and explanation as to the underlining. And if that could be marked Exhibit P2351.4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Good morning, Mr. Treanor. And welcome back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're going to be cross-examined now by Mr. Ackerman who is lead counsel for the Defence, for the accused. The cross-examination is anticipated to go into tomorrow. I don't think we'll finish today. So the shorter your answers, the more precise they are, the quicker you will get out of here. Thank you. So could I ask you to stand up, please. And Madam Registrar is going to hand to you the declaration, solemn declaration, that you are already familiar with. Please go ahead and read it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. So, Mr. Ackerman, it is in your hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Treanor.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So how are you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm fairly well rested, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good. We have, as you might well imagine, a great deal of ground to cover. And I'll just work our way through it as quickly as I can. Although there will be some fairly notable exceptions to this pronouncement that I'm about to make, I intend primarily to work through the events in a chronological fashion. But I want you to understand that I don't intend in that process to provide a complete chronology, but to touch on certain documents and issues that occurred over the period of time we're interested in. I'll be skipping over some other things that occurred which I am not particularly interested in. Do you understand what I'm basically trying to explain to you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to focus almost exclusively on Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the place I want to begin is with amendments that were made to the constitution of that republic in the years 1989 and 1990. And it was these constitutional changes or part of the contents of these constitutional changes that created the conditions under which multiparty elections were eventually held. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In general terms, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm going to be referring several times to Exhibit DB-1, and so I'll ask the Registrar to give a copy of that to you. It's that book right there. Yes, that one. This is a -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you had given this list -- made it available earlier, Mr. Ackerman, we would have had these documents available, too. As it is, we have got two volumes, one of which contains the expert report. The other one, the documents referred to by the Prosecution. And now, we are absolutely unprovided with all the documents practically that you are going to make use of, except those where you overlap with the Prosecution. Anyway, let's go ahead. And my secretary will try to make good for your shortcoming in the break. In the meantime, Madam Registrar, if you could, or Elena, if you could perhaps make a photocopy of this, and hand it to our respective secretaries to have the documents ready by the break, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think we can make quite a lot of use of the ELMO, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. But in the meantime, it's easier, we don't have to stretch our eyes between you, the witness, the ELMO, the Prosecution, your client, and everything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. I wish I could have provided to you earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's go ahead. Let's proceed, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to know if you know about the electoral law which was adopted by the Bosnian parliament in March of 1990 that banned political organisation on the basis of ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm familiar with that law in general terms. I could not bring to mind the specific provisions you're speaking of, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I will not go into the specific provisions. It's just as a general proposition, I take it you'd agree with me that there was an electoral law adopted that attempted to prevent the creation of parties on an ethnic basis, in other words, in other words, the creation of a Muslim or a Serb or a Croat party?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Are were you also aware that the constitutional court then of Bosnia-Herzegovina declared this law unconstitutional, and removed it from the law governing those multiparty elections that occurred later?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And did you know that the President of that constitutional Court was a judge by the name of Dr. Kasim Trnka who later became a very active member of the SDA leadership?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I certainly knew that Dr. Trnka was a member of that court. I can't recall whether I knew he was the president, though. And I know that he was active later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Of the three major parties, the SDA, the HDZ, and the SDS, the first of those to be formed was the SDA, was it not?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that party was formed during the time that the law prohibiting the organisation of parties based on ethnicity was in existence, before it had been declared unconstitutional, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to take your word for that. I believe that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that was a party that was headed by a gentleman by the name of Alija Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the name of that party was such as to not reveal any ethnic basis to it at all; it was I think the Party of democratic action, or something like that, translated, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you know that Alija Izetbegovic had been imprisoned twice under the Tito regime primarily because of his fundamentalist preachings and ideas?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he had been imprisoned. I don't know what the specific charges were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, do you know that the second imprisonment was for circulation of a writing of his called "the Islamic declaration" which he wrote in 1970?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I guess I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Did you know that he represented a faction of the SDA which was inclined toward an identity defined largely in terms of Islam and intent on securing a dominant role for the Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you reading from somewhere, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's actually Exhibit DB-1, page 46, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would you agree with that statement?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me ask you: Just look at the entry on page 46 of DB-1, if we can find it. I can't right now find what I just quoted on page 46.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the bottom of the page perhaps, last paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. In any event, do you agree with that proposition that's stated there?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, quite frankly, I have little basis to either support that or challenge that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's fine. I appreciate that. If you look over on the next page, then, on page 47 --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: At any time Your Honours want, we can put these on the ELMO so you can see them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it would be a better idea, Mr. Ackerman. I understand you have several copies of these.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You're going to be in a position now that you're going to sort of put that over on the ELMO and look at it from that position. So if we'll just put pages 46 and 47 over there so we can see them. And if we could zoom in on the right-hand side with the language "the overtly Islamic..." Is the part -- right in there, yes. "The overtly Islamic and Muslim nationalist orientation of the SDA leadership around Izetbegovic led to a split with the more secular Muslims within the party led by Adil Zulfikarpasic who formed his own party the Muslim Bosniak organisation in October of 1990. Were you aware of that? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I'm aware of some of that in general terms. But I do not have a documentary basis in mind that I could call to support or the refutation of that proposition.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, assuming just for the purposes of the discussion that we're having here now that these statements, these paragraphs that we have been reading from, from DB-1, are correct, these would have been things that would have been known to Serbs, especially those with a political bent, in Bosnia at the time; they would have known about Izetbegovic's imprisonment, his Islamic declaration, his reputation as a relatively militant Muslim? That's not something that would have been a secret, was it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I believe that's correct, again, in general terms. It would have been known to the general public and to the political elite what his background was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And it was probably quite obvious when Zulfikarpasic formed a party with Izetbegovic, what the basis was for his doing that and his concerns about where Izetbegovic was going with the SDA. That probably was also fairly well known, would you think?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that opinions on that would have been current.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So in March of 1990, Izetbegovic starts this SDA party and begins a process of the development of ethnically based parties. There was at the time in Croatia an ethnically based party called the HDZ which later formed its -- an offshoot of it, a party based on the same principles with the same name in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Correct? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you say the same principles, I'm not sure what the principles -- which principles you're referring to, but it certainly had the same name.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. I'll withdraw the principles part and we'll just stick with name. It was a party that was primarily Croat, almost exclusively Croat, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Then finally in July of 1990, finally there was established the SDS party which was a party established under the leadership of Radovan Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the basic platform, the raison d'etre of that party was opposition primarily to Bosnian Independence or to any changes in the makeup of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina that would subject the Serb minority to rule by an ethnically alien majority made up of Muslims and Croats. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, are you reading from DB-1, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would prefer if when you are reading or referring specifically to some part of DB-1, you declare that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could you repeat that or indicate the page where that is found.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If we look at page 47 -- I'm just trying to find it now.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's -- what it reads is: "The Serb Democratic Party" - and it's on your screen, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Down through the words "ethnically alien majority" with the footnote 85 there. That's the passage I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And do you agree with that, or do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think I would have put that proposition in quite those terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Now, with the formation of these parties and the campaigns that followed, there was finally multiparty elections held on 18 November 1990. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And these three ethnic parties, SDA, SDS, HDZ, won the most seats?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Collectively, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The -- for the purposes of that election, the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was divided into seven election districts, was it not?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll take your word for the fact that there were the seven electoral districts for the elections to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Chamber of citizens?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- Chamber of citizens, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You can look at page 50 of DB-1, and we can even put it on the ELMO so the Judges can see, the map that sets out those seven election districts and the number of delegates to be elected from each one. According to the authors, this comes from the writing of Suad Arnautovic that I assume you're familiar with.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Now, there's a new exhibit, DB-160, that was provided this morning. And I'd like you to take a look at that. And you'll actually find it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We don't have this as yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I thought those had all been turned in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This actually comes from DB-1, pages 52 and 53, Your Honours. But I thought it appropriate to make it a separate exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And sir, what you'll see there on Table 2.3 are the results from each of those election districts. And 2.4, the number of seats then distributed based on the outcome of the election.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If we look at first Table 2.3, we find that in Banja Luka, 40 per cent -- 40.85 per cent of the votes went to the SDS. The SDA and HDZ combined got about 33. And the rest was spread among some other minor parties. If you look at Doboj, the SDS got 23 per cent. About 43 per cent was spread between the SDA and the HDZ. And the rest, some of the other parties. Mostar, SDS was a little over 14 per cent, and the SDA and HDZ combined was 78 and a half basically. Sarajevo, SDS 22 per cent; SDA 32 per cent, HDZ about 8 per cent, and the rest other parties, notably SK-SDP, got a higher percentage, as did SRSJ, than the HDZ did. Zenica, the SDS about 9 per cent. About 67 per cent went to HDZ and SDA. Tuzla, SDS about 27 per cent. About 44 and a half per cent went to SDA/HDZ. And finally, Bihac, where the SDS got 21 and a half per cent, that between the HDZ and the SDA, 63 and a half roughly. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what the table shows, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In none of those districts, then, did the SDS over 50 per cent of the vote?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then if you go over and look at Table 2.4, out of the 130 seats, the SDS received less than a third, about 34. Exactly 34. The SDA, 43; and the HDZ, 21. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I offer that as DB-160.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there a document which indicates the turnout of voters?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The turnout --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because I'm impressed by the number of invalid votes which by any standard that I am familiar with is pretty high. And that I take it most of the time to show a deliberate rendering of a vote valid. But I would be interested to know the -- what the turnout was. Because these figures are a percentage of all votes cast, including the invalid votes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know the raw numbers in terms of turnout. Maybe Mr. Treanor does or has access to a document that would show that. Off the top of my head, I don't. It might be in his report. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wouldn't Mr. Treanor to know that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know offhand. We do have the reports of the electoral commission which would, I believe, provide the figures to indicate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Perhaps when you come back tomorrow, you could bring that and we could supply that to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'll look into that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Treanor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I agree with Your Honour, that's a very high number of invalid votes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I'll ask Mr. Treanor if he has any idea why that situation occurred. Do you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do I have any -- I thought you were going to ask me after I'd looked into the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you know now, I'd like to know. If you don't --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could only speculate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. That's probably not a good idea. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. All right. We've already discussed the proposition that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you proceed, Mr. Ackerman, sorry, I would also like to know perhaps either through you Mr. Treanor, or you, Mr. Ackerman after having verified this whether in ex-Yugoslavia at the time, whether voting was statutorily obligatory, as it is in Italy, for example, and in some other countries? Because that could explain the number of invalid votes. But there are some countries in Europe where voting is not just a right, but it is a legal obligation, subject also to penal sanctions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm quite certain that was not the case, but I hunch that's something Mr. Treanor may know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't believe that's the case either, but I can check on that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Treanor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We've already talked a little bit about positions, platforms, what was going on politically with regard to the positions of each of the parties with regard to the question of independence. And I think it's clear that the SDA, supported finally by HDZ, was interested in achieving independence for Bosnia-Herzegovina. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, in general terms, I would say that's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And very soon after these multiparties, the SDA tried to get a declaration of sovereignty through the Bosnian assembly. That would have been in November 1991, and failed in their efforts at the time. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with that document. And my answer to the previous question, I didn't realise you were trying to gear that to the electoral period. I'm not certain what their position was at that particular time, that is, in the pre-electoral campaign.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, let's at least go to February of 1991, shortly after those elections when an effort was made to get a declaration of sovereignty through the Bosnian Assembly by the SDA, which failed. And my source for that, if you look at DB-1, page 71, the second -- the beginning of the second full paragraph. And maybe you can slide that over to the ELMO so the -- starts with the language "in February, and then again in May..." Needs to be brought down and to the left just a tad.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Has to be moved to page 71, and then up. Up. There. "In February, and then again in May 1991, the SDA attempted to push a declaration of sovereignty through the Bosnian Assembly. Both resolutions failed."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you have any reason to doubt the accuracy of that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in substance, no. Again, I'm not sure I would have put that proposition in that manner, "push."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. You might quarrel with the word "push." Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Now, this was apparently happening in the parliament, the assembly, in February and May. In April of 1991, after the February activity in the parliament and before that, in May, the community of Bosnian Krajina Municipalities was formed, was it not?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In April, yes, April, May. Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. And that is Exhibit P69. And I'd like you to be furnished that so you can just take a look at that, a little part of it I want you to see. If you look at Article 9, which is on page 3, this is a section which deals with all-people's defence. "In the area of all-people's defence and social self-protection in its territory, the community of municipalities shall..." And then it sets out a number of things that the community shall do. "In a time of war, threat of war, to organise the all-people's defence in the territory of the community of municipalities. To organise the all-people's defence in the community of municipalities and to lead it. Talks about preparations, organisation, things like that, of all-people's defence. This is a -- all-people's defence was basically a municipality obligation in terms of administration and organisation up to that point, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think I would describe it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How would you describe it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an obligation in a -- including a financial obligation, an organisational obligation, which was in the responsibility of the individual republics. And many of theses activities and responsibilities were devolved to the municipalities. I would not say it was basically a municipal function, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But each of the municipalities had responsibilities regarding the all-people's defence, the TO?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the area of their municipalities, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the community of municipalities that is formed here is just making an effort to coordinate the responsibilities of the municipalities regarding these issues, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, you've said "just." I'm not sure what you mean by just.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Leave out the words of just --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The text of the article purports to claim a role in that regard that is set out in the article, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, at page 5 of your report, you describe this community of Bosnian Krajina Municipalities as having been formed by a number of SDS-dominated municipalities in northwest Bosnia. That's your language, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, would you agree --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's page 5 of the...?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Page 5 of your report in this case.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The addendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, there's some confusion about that because your original report is called "the addendum." It's a report that you filed in this case, you prepared for this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's called the addendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour, but so is his original report.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: His original report is called the Bosnian Serb leadership 1990-1993, dated the 30th of July, 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There's no purpose in this argument. When the Prosecution submitted the original report, they called it an addendum to their submission of the expert witness, and that's why I use the word addendum because the Prosecution called it that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The report is called an addendum because it's an addendum to this report that I just referred to, which is Exhibit P2352 and the addendum is Exhibit P2353.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It is a waste of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed. It's neither fish nor fowl. And what's in a name anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, you're correct. As long as he knows what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know which document we're talking about, Mr. Treanor?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I've found page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you've found the language I'm referring to?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is it in paragraph E5?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It's about halfway through paragraph E5 where it says "in the early months of 1991 following the multiparty elections and the establishment of Municipal Assembly Assemblies dominated by one or another of the nationally based parties, including the Serbian democratic party, a number of SDS dominated municipalities in northwest Bosnia established the community of the municipalities of the Bosnian Krajina."

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, my question to you is that is not a completely accurate statement, is it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you'd like to call my attention to the -- some part you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. disagree with, I'd be willing to go into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I will. If you look at the list of municipalities that were part of this agreement, you'll find, for instance, the municipality of Kotor Varos; you'll find the municipality of Sanski Most. And I think you'll agree that neither of those were SDS-dominated municipalities, won't you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't have the figures or facts in front of me in regards to those municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Maybe I can help you just a little bit. And maybe not much, but maybe a little bit. If you look at Exhibit P58, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Ackerman please slow down when he reads the text. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you look at page 4, you'll see Kotor Varos, in 1991, at least 38 per cent of the people living there were Serbs. And about 59 and a half per cent were Muslims and Croats. So I think it's possible to infer, at least, that the municipality was not SDS-dominated. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that basis, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If we look at Sanski Most, and that's on page 8, at least in 1991 population was about 42 per cent Serb. And about 54 per cent Muslim and Croat. So again, we might infer that that was not an SDS-dominated municipality.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that would be a reasonable assumption on the basis of those figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, if we look now at Exhibit P2354 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, I'm sorry to interrupt you in the course of your cross-examination. But while this document is being checked by the witness, I am informed, and I did have some indication before that as well, that before you tendered the first of today's documents, Defence documents, DB-160, the last document that you had tendered and was admitted before was DB-149. So there seems to be from DB-150 to 159 unaccounted for.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are they going to be documents related to the witness we should have had yesterday and the day before?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, but we will eventually fill those in. What happened is we were trying to reach the Registrar, Chuqing, to try to get what our last exhibit number was and we were unable to do so. Therefore, as an abundance of caution, we decided to start with 160 and then fill in whatever was missing later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will retain --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We won't change those, and we will try to those numbers as we go along. We just weren't able to get that number yesterday, and we had to make designations. So that's the explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We're now looking at P2354 -- do you still have P69 there with you, too, the one we were just looking at? Because I think it might be useful for you to look at those two together. I would like to point out for the Chamber, sir, that Prijedor Municipality was not part of this agreement on the formation of the community of Bosnian Krajina Municipalities, was it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Was Prijedor part -- I don't believe so, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The problem here, as with -- as is sometimes a problem elsewhere is there are various documents that bear on the question of which municipalities were, in fact, members of this community of municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think we're getting to what you're getting to rather rapidly. That's why I'm asking you to look at 21. As Exhibit 2354, this is the statute of that same association, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And if you compare the two in that original document, the agreement on the formation, P69, there were 19 municipalities that were part of that. When we get to the constitution, that number has dropped to 16. In neither of those is there a Prijedor. And in the second document, P2354, the municipalities of Kotor Varos and Sanski Most are also no longer involved. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I think that's what you were trying to point out.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would point out in that regard that there are two versions of the agreement to form the community which have different -- differ between themselves as to which municipalities are involved. And then this document basically includes the 16 municipalities that were common to the two lists of municipalities in those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And what you just pointed out is not a completely unusual state of affairs with the documents that have come out of former Yugoslavia. Sometimes there are multiple versions of a document that differ, aren't there?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I think as we go through some more documents here today or tomorrow, we're going to see at least one or two more examples of that, which makes drawing conclusions about some things rather difficult, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That depends on the conclusion you want to draw.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I assume that the conclusion that you want to draw is always the one most favourable to the accused since that's what the law would require you to do.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that the law requires me to do anything other than make my best effort to interpret these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I take it that you do --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The issue --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- You do want the Court to see you here as an unbiased, independent, expert witness, and not as a representative of the Office of the Prosecutor, or would you rather be seen as an advocate of the Office of the Prosecutor? Which of those would you prefer?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well again, the terms that you put the issue in are not the terms that I would use.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What would you use?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say I am here to enlighten the Court and help in any way I can to understand the documents that have been put before it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In that process, in your report, you arrive at a significant number of conclusions based upon the documents that you've reviewed, don't you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And when more than one conclusion is possible from a document, one consistent with the Prosecutor's allegations in the indictment and one inconsistent with it, don't you tend to always favour the conclusion that supports the indictment?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not say that that is invariably correct. I think we endeavour to make the best-founded conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This document you have before you now, P2354, I'd like you to look at Article 5 first, please. Article 5 provides that "the official language of the association of municipalities organs shall be Serbo-Croatian and Croato-Serbian using the Cyrillic or Latin alphabets." Does that have any significance in your mind?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you proceed, Mr. Ackerman, and before he answers that question, because I think we need to clarify this, you previously asked the witness "and when more than one conclusion is possible from a document, one consistent with the Prosecutor's allegations in the indictment and one inconsistent with it, don't you tend to always favour the conclusion that supports the indictment?" And the witness answered: "I would not say that that is invariably correct. I think we endeavour to make the best-founded conclusion." I think we need to clarify the position both as regards your question and as regards his answer. He is a witness, for all intents and purposes an expert appointed by the Prosecution. So I want to know from the witness whether he feels that as a Prosecution expert witness, he has any duties towards the Prosecution to present their case from a scientific research point of view as a stronger case. And I want a clear-cut answer from you, sir. For all intents and purposes, you are an ex parte witness -- expert witness. You are not an independent expert appointed by the Tribunal or by the Trial Chamber. You have been appointed by the Prosecution and brought forward as a Prosecution witness, expert witness. So in your report, did you take that into consideration? Did you feel it was your duty to bring out all the evidence that would support the Prosecution's case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me back up a little bit to answer that. I can say it is my professional obligation, be it to the Office of the Prosecutor or be it to this Court, to objectively evaluate the documents which are available to me and to draw the most reasonable conclusions from those documents. I would not be serving the -- either the Office of the Prosecutor or this Court well by telling the Prosecution what it wanted to hear. My job is to, again, look at all available documents, endeavour to collect documents which I believe would be helpful and are missing to us, and to analyse and evaluate those documents objectively. The report was written on that basis. Everything we write in my section is written on that basis. And I conceive it as my duty to the Office of the Prosecutor as well as to this Court to present an objective view of what the documents say. To do anything else would not be serving either the Prosecutor or the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I'm happy with that answer, Mr. Treanor. Thank you. Mr. Ackerman, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And can we go back to the question that you asked before.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'll just ask it again, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We were looking at Article 5, Mr. Treanor.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the question I asked you was: "Do you see any significance in the language of Article 5"?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would say that Article 5 states the position on the use of language that was current in the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Right. And you know that the SDS position, at least as later expressed, was that the only appropriate alphabet was Cyrillic?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know they certainly made efforts in that direction, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Look also at Article 11. Article 11 provides at the very beginning, the first sentence: "Each member municipality may leave the association of municipalities." To me this signifies that what we've got here is a voluntary association, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You can be a member, a municipality can be a member if it wishes; it can not be a member if it wishes; it can come in and go back out at will. There are some regulations on how you go about doing that, but it's a voluntary association?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Right. And finally Article 16 deals with this same issue of all-people's defence that we talked about a few moments ago. And what this says is that: "The association of municipalities shall monitor the situation and coordinate activities for the organisation and implementation of preparations for all-people's defence in accordance with the law, municipal defence plans, and the republican defence plan." Right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the republican defence plan it's referring to is that of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And this association was formed, if you look at the preamble, pursuant to -- I think it's amendment 42, if I can read Roman numerals properly, to the constitution of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and Article 4 of the agreement on uniting the association of municipalities of 14 May 1991. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So it was formed under the republican constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Not under the Serbian Republic or anything like that. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And a regional community like this that was formed under the constitution of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, these were not sociopolitical communities, were they?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The communities of municipalities, that is correct, they were not what are termed in Yugoslavia political parlance, legal parlance, a sociopolitical community.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And in that legal parlance, could you tell the Chamber what is meant by "sociopolitical community" or "sociopolitical" --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my understanding, that term is used to denote what I would call governmental units, beginning with the local communities, then the municipalities, the republics themselves, and the federation, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In fact, the constitutional court of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina specifically ruled on 1 November 1991 that defence is organised only by sociopolitical communities; that is, by the republican municipalities, not by communities of municipalities because they lack that characteristic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's a little bit early, but there's a major break here and I think it might make sense to take the break now rather than later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No problem at all, Mr. Ackerman. We'll have a break of 25 minutes, resuming at quarter to 11.00. Quarter to 11.00. Thank you

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman, you may proceed. But before you do so, I noticed that in the schedule that you handed to us this morning, there's a reference to the cross-examination of the witness we should have cross-examined yesterday and the day before.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And that's scheduled for the -- starting 3rd of November. Is that in agreement with the Prosecution, or is it just a suggestion on your part?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's mostly what will work best for us, Your Honour. The Prosecution would like to have him here a little earlier. But we've already made some significant arrangements regarding these first few witnesses. So we prefer to do it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. I've spoken with Mr. Ackerman, said we would prefer to do that sooner rather than later and finish off that witness. But we don't object to that date if Mr. Ackerman tells us that it's the only real way he can do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you want to take both of you to come back to this later on once you have decided -- taken a decision as to when that gentleman is coming over to be cross-examined?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think we're both comfortable with leaving it where it is at this point, Your Honour, if it's okay with the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is okay with the Court. I just wanted to know whether it's just an initiative on your part. So let's proceed with Mr. Treanor. Mr. Ackerman, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, we had been talking before the break about the association of municipalities of Bosanska Krajina, what has been referred to many times in this case as ZOBK. We were looking at the statute of 14 May 1991. About four months later, 16 September 1991, this association transformed itself into the Autonomous Region of Krajina. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let's look at Exhibit P81, please. Now, we're in September of 1991. This is before the October events in the republican assembly regarding the question of independence, when the Serbs walked out of the assembly and there was a vote. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is before October 1991, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. I guess that was a fairly obvious question, wasn't it? The word "autonomous," you see it in the first page there under the title "decision," "on the proclamation of the Autonomous Region of Krajina." That was a deliberately used word, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I presume that they deliberately chose that word.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you look at Articles 8 and 9, one might get a clue as to why the word "autonomous" was chosen. Article 8 reads: "If the constitutional/legal position of BH in federal state of Yugoslavia changes, the assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina will decide to form a separate republic on its own or together with other republics, which would become a federal republic and a part of the federal state of Yugoslavia." They then say they're going to send this decision, the one we're reading, to the assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina for adoption, and that if it fails to be adopted by the Assembly of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, a decision for separation would then be submitted to the association for adoption, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: To add to it, I would refer the witness to the preamble which is very clear in the terminology used there, it says: "Precisely pursuant to every nation's right to self-determination," so we're talking of an Autonomous Region of Krajina, referring to "every nation's right to self-determination, including the right to secession, based upon its freely expressed will and in accordance with its historical aspirations to live united in the federal state of the federative Yugoslavia," which is implying -- that's it. And then it's the decision. So you have the macrocosm becoming the microcosm or vice versa.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So what's going on here is basically the beginning of a separatist movement basically, that if you don't adopt what we're suggesting here, then, you know, we're going to create our own republic, the republic of whatever, Bosanska Krajina or whatever you want to call it. Right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would describe this as an important step in a secessionist movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that secessionist movement is based upon the proposition that there is a movement by the SDA to create an independent state of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't say that here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But that was the underlying political reality, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me say, my understanding of the underlying political reality which -- based on the documents which I have read, first of all, that a context which you provided going to the future about this decision, but going a little bit into the past, it's useful to recall that the Republics of Slovenia and Croatia declared their independence at the end of June 1991, and that hostilities in those republics began shortly thereafter. And in the case of Croatia, continued at least through the end of and probably after the end of the year. So that the political situation within Yugoslavia as a whole had drastically changed. Prior to that time, there may have been hope and effort, indeed there were efforts to keep the whole country together. This was undermined by the events I just described. And I believe it's correct to say that the Croatian democratic community, that is the Croatian-based political party in Bosnia and Herzegovina was no longer interested in having Bosnia-Herzegovina remain within Yugoslavia, but rather were interested in some sort of association with Croatia, which had declared itself independent. And that this situation impacted on the position of the SDA as well in a similar direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, yeah, and as long as you've decided to talk about those events, especially the events that happened in Slovenia and Croatia and the hostilities that broke out there, that was all for the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina, not just the Serbs, but all the citizens, that was a fairly anxiety producing series of events, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. Keep that document that you have, and I'd ask that you now be given P80, because this is another one of those sort of curious things that we were talking about earlier. The first document, the P81 that we have been talking about, is dated 16 September 1991. And then immediately on the same day, there seems to have been adopted a statute of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. I think you expressed the opinion at some point that it's unlikely that both of those things happened on the same day, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I expressed that opinion. I think that the date of the adoption of the statute is a little fuzzy, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In any event, there is a statute that was adopted, isn't there? And that's Exhibit P80.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, Prijedor Municipality is still not involved, if you look at Article 1 of the statute of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. Right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. There's no mention of Prijedor here. I only have the translation in front of me, I don't have the original. But on the basis of the translation, yes, Prijedor is not mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you look at the preamble, again, this statute is based on the authority of that same amendment, 42, to the constitution of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Article 1 says that these municipalities that are listed there have united on the basis of voluntariness, solidarity, equality, and for the purpose of effecting permanent cooperation, harmonisation of development plans, and the realisation of other common interests.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The language in my translation is a little different from that we see on the screen, which probably is a more recent translation. But in any event, that's the basic idea. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If we look at Article 4, Article 4 reads: "In performing tasks within the jurisdiction of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, all peoples and nationalities in the Autonomous Region of Krajina shall have equal rights and duties, without distinction as to race, sex, birth, language, nationality, religion, political or other beliefs, education, social background, wealth, and any other personal qualities." True?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And again, we're talking about a voluntary association of municipalities, aren't we?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Also, in Article 5, there's that same expression regarding language, the official language of the Autonomous Region of Krajina shall be either Serbo-Croatian or Croato-Serbian using the Cyrillic or Latin alphabets.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's identical to the language that was in the ZOBK document that we looked at earlier, I think.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those two documents, that is, this statute and the other statute, are almost identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you look at Article 11, right there at the top of the page, the same language again: "Each member municipality may leave the Autonomous Region of Krajina." In other words, they can separate from this voluntary association. There are some regulations as to how they go about doing that. But again, it's the same kind of languages as in the ZOBK document. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to look now at Article 35. And I think if nothing else, this highlights the completely voluntary nature of this association. If you look at the second paragraph of Article 35: "Decisions and conclusions of the Assembly shall become binding for the member municipalities once they have been approved by the assemblies of municipalities."

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In other words, the decisions and conclusions of the ARK assembly were only binding on municipalities once their own assemblies accepted them.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. We're going to go now to the 14th and 15th of October of 1991. This was a day of what I'm calling a showdown in the assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And I think the Chamber is aware of some fairly well-known speeches made that day by Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Izetbegovic. And you know what I'm talking about, don't you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. The session of the assembly --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- Of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina took place on that day. I believe it had begun a couple of days earlier, in fact. It may have stretched into the 15th.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It did, indeed. I think they were in session for hours. There's a description of it, and I'm not going to refer to it, language. But there's a description of it on page 77 of this DB-1, of that meeting. But I think for the purposes of our discussion this morning, what happened was the Muslims and -- the Serbs abandoned the assembly, the Muslims and Croats convened a rump session of the assembly and adopted a declaration of sovereignty by a majority vote.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in general terms, yes. Again, I wouldn't use quite that language to describe what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And in any event, the issue then of sovereignty passed by this rump session of the assembly without participation of the Serbs then prompted a request by the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina to the European community for recognition as an independent state? And that went off to a commission called the Badinter Commission. Right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In general terms, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Could you explain for the Chamber what was the Badinter Commission, just so we have that in the record if it's not already there.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I recollect correctly, the Commission was set up by the European Community, as it was at that time, to review the situation in the former Yugoslavia, in particular, the individual republics in connection with their movements toward independence and to make recommendations to those republics and to the European Community as a whole, the government of the European Community in connection with, if I may put it, application for independence, recognition of independence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Application for recognition of independence. After this showdown of the 14th and the 15th of October in the assembly, the Serbs then decided to hold a plebiscite of the Serbian people to try to accurately determine the will of the Serbian people regarding this issue of independence. Did they want to be part of an independent nation, or did they want to remain part of Yugoslavia? And this plebiscite was held on the 9th and 10th of November, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that's correct. I would have thought it was the 10th and the 11th, but maybe you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you might be right. I think it's the 9th and 10th, though. Let's look at -- I hope I have it. I may not have it. We're going to look at this document, we're going to have to look at it tomorrow because I think I neglected to bring it. There's a report written by the Commission of Experts that details this plebiscite. And according to that report, on page 24, there was about an 85 per cent turnout of eligible voters; 95 per cent of whom voted in favour of remaining within the Federal State of Yugoslavia. Does that square with your knowledge about --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That sounds about right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to look then -- now, after that plebiscite, then, and after that vote and after -- we'll look at DB-161, and then I'll ask you some more questions about it. Now, DB-161 is the opinion on international recognition of the socialist republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina by the European Community and its member states issued in Paris on 11 January, 1992. First of all, it states that on 20 November, 1991, a letter was written to the president of the council of European Communities by the minister of foreign affairs of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina asking the member states of the European Community to recognise Bosnia-Herzegovina as an independent state. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then there's a lot of language about that process. And we finally get over to the third page, paragraphs 3 and 4. About halfway down in paragraph 3, the following language appears: "Outside the institutional framework of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina on 10 November 1991, the Serbian people of Bosnia-Herzegovina voted in a plebiscite for a common Yugoslav state. On 21 December 1991, an assembly of the Serbian people of Bosnia-Herzegovina passed a resolution calling for the formation of a Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in a federal Yugoslav state if the Muslim and Croat communities of Bosnia and Herzegovina decided to change their attitude towards Yugoslavia. On 9 January 1992, this Assembly proclaimed the independent of a Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." And then this, paragraph 4: "In these circumstances, the arbitration commission is of the opinion that the will of the peoples of Bosnia and Herzegovina to constitute the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina as a sovereign and independent state cannot be held to have been fully established. "This assessment could be reviewed if appropriate guarantees were provided by the Republic applying for recognition, possibly by means of a referendum of all the citizens of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina without distinction, carried out under international supervision." Now, it appears that what the Badinter Commission is telling the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina is "we can't approve your application for independence when one of your constituent nations, the Serbian people, appear to be completely opposed to it. So maybe what you can do is hold a referendum and show us that all of the citizens, without distinction, would be in favour of this application." That's a fair reading of that, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This referendum was then, in fact, held on 29 February and 1 March of 1992, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
