utterances.text: And in that referendum, 63.4 per cent of the electorate voted, 99 per cent of them in favour of independence?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll certainly take your word on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And this referendum was openly boycotted by at least large numbers, if not somewhere around 95 per cent of the Serbs, very small number of Serbs voted in other words.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. The SDS in fact ordered Serbs not to vote.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. Would you agree that if the fact of that earlier plebiscite and the expressed will of the Serbian people in that earlier plebiscite was sufficient to convince the Badinter Commission that the will of the people of Bosnia-Herzegovina had not been appropriately expressed in favour of independence, that it made some sense that a complete boycott of the referendum by one of these constituent peoples would underscore that lack of will and perhaps make it even clearer to the Badinter Commission that one of the constituent peoples was very opposed to that proposition?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have thought that that is the conclusion that they would draw, that one of the peoples was opposed to that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And this was done in a context that those of us from the outside may not have a full appreciation of. This was done in a context of a country that since World War II, and the government of Tito, had been very - what's the best way to put this? - the rights of these constituent people, the rights of these minority ethnicities had been very heavily protected and heavily secured throughout this whole period so that one of the constituent peoples, if one of the constituent peoples objected to something that was going on in that country and in the assemblies and in the SFRY or in one of the republics, that certain things simply couldn't happen over their objection. There was the kljuc system, there were provisions in the constitution, everything else --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly agree that there was very heavy emphasis in the communist period on the existence of the nations and nationalities and their rights, et cetera, et cetera. However, there was no mechanism by which those - let's just stick to the nations - per se could express their will or view on any matter. The only way that that could happen was through the people -- the officials, deputies in the assembly, government officials, members of the presidency, et cetera, who happened to be members of those nationalities, as you mentioned, the key, the kljuc, which was a mechanism to guarantee that each nation or nationality had adequate representation within the various organs of government. But it was only through those organs that they could express their will -- or a political will could be expressed at all. The system did not have a mechanism that permitted the nations per se to express their will independently of the existing organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah, except there was -- because of the way the system was designed, it was designed to prevent, say, the Serbs and the Croats from getting together and ganging up on the Muslims and taking away their rights or any of the groups to get together and attack a minority and take away the rights of that minority. I mean, that really was how that process was designed, the government was designed, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're going a little far afield here. I think in general terms, that's certainly one of the purposes. I think the main purpose of the system was to guarantee the continuous power of the communists.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you know that in July 1990, an amendment, there was an amendment adopted to the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina which created a council -- it has a horrible name. A Council for questions of the establishment of equality of the nations and nationalities of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And this council was designed to consistent of an equal number of Croats, Serbs, and Muslims, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And by its provisions of this amendment, if 20 deputies to the assembly considered that an act of the assembly undermined the equality of nations, then it would be sent off to this body for consideration. And then this council could propose that for the act to be adopted, a two-thirds majority would be necessary.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And this was simply a continued recognition of the necessity of protecting the rights of the constituent peoples, the minority peoples.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And it sought to provide the mechanism which I mentioned earlier was lacking in the previous system.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And if we -- the previous system, I guess the reason for that was the previous system didn't have these multiple parties that we wound up with by this time?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. It was not a multiparty system.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: During those debates that we were talking about on the 14th and 15th of October on the independence resolutions in the republic assembly, Serbs requested that that issue be referred to this council that you and I have just been discussing, and the Muslim/Croat representatives voted against that and prevented it from being sent off to this council on the grounds that the council had not yet been constituted.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to switch to another document now. This is a document that we've heard a lot about in this case. It's P25, Exhibit P25. And we refer to it generically as the "variant A and B document." Now, at this point, the independence issue has passed the assembly and has been sent off to the European Community requesting recognition. There has been the plebiscite of the Serbian people. But it's still 1991. It's 19 December of 1991. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And we know that that letter that we referred to that was sent off to the European Community requesting recognition was done clearly against the will of the Serb people of Bosnia-Herzegovina which was pretty clearly expressed. Right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, it was clearly against the will of the Serbian democratic party, and the will of the Serbian people as expressed at that plebiscite.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let's look at the first page now of this variant A/B document. First of all, I think it's important that we keep in mind that what they are called is "instructions." And then you look at this first paragraph, there, number 1 "these instructions have been prepared because of a justifiable suspicion that certain forces are operating in a persistent, thorough, and organised manner toward the forcible removal of Bosnia-Herzegovina and thereby the Serbian people from Yugoslavia. The instructions elaborate uniform tasks, measures, and activities..." And remember "tasks, measures, and activities" because I think that's also important. "... which will be carried out within the national community of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina for the purpose of carrying out the results of the plebiscite at which the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina decided to live in a single state both under the existing conditions and circumstances and all such conditions that may arise given the current political and security developments". Number two: "The tasks, measures, and activities that are laid out in these instructions will be carried out in order to increase mobility and readiness for the defence of the interests of the Serbian people." So we're speaking about the things that are contained in the rest of this document, as tasks, measures, and activities, that will be carried out at some point. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, back to that page 5 of your report, in paragraph E6, you make this statement, first sentence: "Beginning in December 1991, the SDS ordered the establishment of bodies known as Crisis Staffs in all municipalities in which Bosnian Serbs lived." That's what you told this Court, this Chamber, in your report. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And would I be correct in the assumption that when you wrote this sentence, that you were referring to this document we have now before us, this variant A/B document?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And more specifically, referring to page 3, paragraph 3, and the page 6, paragraph 3 of the document which says "the SDS municipal board will immediately form a Crisis Staff of the Serbian people in the municipality comprised of the following..."

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. That's one of the tasks that page 2 refers to when it talks about tasks, measures, and activities, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: One of the tasks being to form a Crisis Staff of the Serbian people. Yes?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want you to look now at the very last page of this document. And it's a bit ambiguous. But paragraph 3 and 4 at the bottom read as follows: "The order to carry out the specified tasks, measures, and other activities in these instructions is given exclusively by the BH SDS president using a secret, pre-established procedure." And then number 4: "The secret procedure for transmitting and accepting the order to carry out the tasks, measures, and other activities specified in these instructions shall be established at a future time."

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Are you aware of any order from Karadzic which ordered the carrying out of any of the tasks, measures, and activities contained in this document?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to answer that question, I think I'd have to go beyond -- may have to go beyond the documentation which is adduced in those reports. I think there is reference in the report - and by the report, I mean what I call the first report, not the addendum --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In this document, what --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, let me complete the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that there was in fact a meeting of SDS officials, I believe it was the day after the date this document refers. I believe it was the day after the date that this document bears, the 20th, perhaps the 21st of December. One of the large-type meetings that Karadzic was wont to call at which this document was distributed. There's a reference of that meeting in the diary of Karadzic's chef du cabinet. What went on at the meeting per se is not documented. On the 14th of February, there was another large meeting which was alluded to in my testimony, and at that meeting there was a speech given by Karadzic in which he referred to implementing the second degree of the instructions. Now, I put that together with the fact that we have documentation indicating that Crisis Staffs -- documentation and other evidence indicating that Crisis Staffs - some Crisis Staffs - were, in fact, formed during the period between the 19th of December and indeed the 14th of February. I put these facts together to draw the conclusion that at some point in time after the 19th of December and before the 14th of February, the local -- the municipal SDS officials were, in fact, instructed -- believe they had been instructed, at least, to form Crisis Staffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: What the secret procedure is, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There's nowhere in this document that there's anything called the second degree, is there?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I mean, that language doesn't appear in here.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It occurs in two places, if I can peruse the translation. I can see why you're puzzled. Under II, discussion of variant A, in the Serbo-Croatian, the next following line has the words which I would translate as "first degree." Stepen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Give me the words.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prva stepen. It's translated here as first stage. An alternate translation of that word would be degree. We then see --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- the question becomes. I'll accept that from you. You don't have to go show me any more. The question becomes that you were talking about a speech made by Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In which you say that Karadzic said something about the second degree.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And notes made by participants at that meeting used the same used.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What I'm interested in is the word that Karadzic used at that time. Did he use that word "stepen"?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so. I can't call the passage to mind. I do know that in notes of participants that they made later, they do use that word. They adduced those --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you have it there?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We can get the speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's now another task that I'll ask you to try to perform before tomorrow. I think it would be interesting to use the word stepen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think we need to postpone it until tomorrow. Can I ask Mr. Nicholls or Ms. Sutherland to try and find it, locate it, please now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: While we're looking for that, let me have another look at another document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You should have it handy. We have it in both languages, both in English and in B/C/S, Ms. Sutherland. I think -- I don't know who would have it handy

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'm just trying to find it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: While we're doing that, can we look at DB-162.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the part of this document that I'm interested in is on page 23. Now, this is the 14th session of the Assembly of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina of 27 March of 1992, three months after this variant A/B document was leased which you say ordered the establishment of Crisis Staffs in all the municipalities. Three months later, here's Karadzic speaking at the assembly. If you look near the bottom of page 23: "When you return to your municipalities, especially the newly formed municipalities, I ask you to do what you're entitled under the law. The moment you arrive in your municipalities, you must urgently establish Crisis Staffs." Right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, if he ordered them to do that in December of 1991, why on earth is he in March of 1992 telling them to go home and establish Crisis Staffs? That makes no sense, unless he ignored his earlier order, or if it wasn't an order. I mean, which is which here?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, I can only draw an inference, and I can understand why you're puzzled. My inference would be that in fact not all municipalities, not all SDS municipal organisations had formed Crisis Staffs, and that he was urging them to get going.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But you told this Chamber in your report, the SDS ordered the establishment of bodies known as Crisis Staffs in all municipalities in December 1991. And you told us that variant A/B is an order to establish Crisis Staffs. And what I'm suggesting to you, it isn't that at all. It's a document saying that here's some things we will do in the future when I decide to do them and let you know secretly to implement them. I think that's what that document is. And this, I think, confirms that. It's not until Martha Karadzic says, okay, go off and form Crisis Staffs.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's because of the intervening facts that I mentioned earlier that I would interpret this differently, that I mentioned the fact that Crisis Staffs had been created in certain areas before this. This indicates to me that they had not been formed in all municipalities. It's correct he had given an order, but the order hadn't been carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So your position is that people were ignoring Karadzic, municipalities were ignoring Karadzic, not --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: My position is, yes, it looks like in this case that his order was not carried out, had not been carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So there was no -- this was no tight SDS organisation, enterprise, marching in lockstep, everything doing what they were ordered too? Of course people were ignoring the orders of Karadzic at their will with no apparent punishment for doing so? If it's your position that he told them in December 1991 to form Crisis Staffs and they didn't do so, then they were just free to ignore him?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of this, I would certainly conclude that in some municipalities, and I don't know how many, Crisis Staffs had not been formed. To make a sweeping generalisation of that nature on the basis of this, I think, may be going too far. However, if we look at other evidence, I think it is certainly true that Karadzic had to do a lot of cajoling - if I may use that word - a lot of talking to get people to carry out various instructions. He put a lot of energy into doing that. And he would intervene in certain cases, move people, that sort of thing. He had a hard job.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He was ignored a lot, wasn't he? I mean I've got some more examples we'll see today.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, "a lot," statistically, I don't know. But it's certainly true that he had to intervene in many cases to see that previous instructions had been carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It would certainly be very hard to conclude that the SDS was some sort of organisation operating in clockwork fashion, everybody carrying out orders and doing what they were being told to do, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would not describe it in that fashion. It was an organisation of like-minded individuals who had their own interests, competencies, and this, that, and the other thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Apparently not like-minded, because what one of them wanted done, the others ones weren't doing. One of the leaders wanted Crisis Staffs in December 1991, according to you, and several of them, the followers, said, "no." And so he had to tell them as late as March 1992, he had to go and tell them again: Go home and create Crisis Staffs. Come on, I'm getting tired of this.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to enter into a polemic on this issue since it's an interpretive matter. There are other reasons, incompetence to lack of energy and what not as to why things weren't done.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Let's go back to this variant A/B document. I want you to go back and just revisit those two paragraphs at the end, paragraphs 3 and 4. And keep in mind where we are in chronological order here, we are in between the October activities in the assembly and the letter that was sent by the government to the European Community requesting recognition of independence. We are in between those incidents and the decision of the Badinter Commission saying "no, we don't believe that there is sufficient indication of the will of the people to agree to grant independence at the present time." We're between those events with this document, aren't we?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me suggest this to you, let me suggest to you that this document was created as a basis for a possible reaction in the event independence was granted by the European Community, that it was never intended to have any effect on December 19th, 1991, and that's why paragraphs 3 and 4 are there. These are things that will be done if certain other things happen. And if I want any of those things carried out, then I, as President of SDS, will secretly advise you by a procedure that will be set up in the future. In other words, this document orders nothing. It's just a blueprint for what might have to be done if independence is granted, a preparatory document. Doesn't that make more sense?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's certainly one interpretation. But again, I take the document together with other events that occurred at that time, most notably the meeting of the SDS leadership the day after the issue -- the document is dated. And the fact that Crisis Staffs in some areas, at least, and again, we don't have complete documentation on every area as to when Crisis Staffs were established, as evidence that the instruction where is carried out. They are called instructions. Whether you want to characterise this as an order or not is, in my opinion, a semantic issue. I mean, they provided the instructions, the guidelines, and apparently within a day or two of the instructions being drawn up, they were distributed to the local and other SDS leaders and told to get going.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, you don't have any evidence for the told to get going part at all?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Crisis Staffs were established.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You have no evidence that they were told to get going. The document speaks for itself. I mean, anybody-- if this was distributed to somebody, they should read paragraphs 3 and 4, and give them meaning, shouldn't they?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as I say, there was a meeting where this was distributed, and after that meeting, Crisis Staffs were established.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I mean, that's -- if you were to say publicly tomorrow "I think Yasar Arafat ought to get out of Palestine," and three days later he leaves Palestine, I take it you wouldn't take credit for him leaving?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're not getting into that analogy now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You're making a linkage here --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Charges --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't answer that question, Mr. Treanor. Because it captious one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I mean you can't conclude because someone makes a statement and then something follows from that statement that it was the result of the statement unless you have some evidence to show that. You don't have any evidence that anybody created a Crisis Staff because of this document, do you?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think Mr. Treanor has already answered this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Pardon? I will allow it. Answer it once for all and, Mr. Treanor, and let's move forward.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are references in later documentation to this instruction which would make it appear that this instruction was being followed. As to when precisely the incident in time was that these instructions were carried out, to use the term here, when the order was given, in terms of paragraph 3, the order was given, I don't have a document that shows that. But we know that there was a meeting within a day or two of the instructions being drawn up, the instructions were distributed. And very shortly thereafter, we see the creation of Crisis Staffs in certain areas, and we see references to the instructions being made in various contexts, including the 14 February speech, et cetera. So in my conclusion, based on all those facts, and there may be other evidence that I'm unaware of, is that Crisis Staffs were set up on the basis of these instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, we're going to explore that. You used some language. I'm going to quote it exactly. "There are references in later documentation to this instruction which would make it appear that this instruction was being followed." I worry about language like "make it appear" when we are operating in a forum where there must be proof beyond a reasonable doubt. I think appearances don't meet that standard. Don't you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Paragraph 4: "The secret procedure for transmitting and accepting the order to carry out the tasks, measures, and other activities specified in these instructions shall be established at a future time." Do you know of any evidence that would indicate, that would prove, that that procedure was ever established?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, you believe, because Crisis Staffs were established, that it must have been because of this document, at least that's the conclusion you draw. Let's test that a little bit. Go back to page 6, paragraph 3. "The SDS municipal board will immediately form a Crisis Staff of the Serbian people in the municipality..." And then it talks about who shall be part of that Crisis Staff. All members of the SDS municipal board secretariat. All executive officials in the municipality, SDS candidates and all municipal bodies. Representatives in the assembly of the Serbian people of BH. Members of the BH SDS main board from that municipality. So it says "set up the Crisis Staff. These will be the members." Do you know of a Crisis Staff that was set up in any municipality that had the membership set out in that manner? Do you know of one?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Set out in those terms?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of any documents that would do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Let's look at the next sentence?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Ackerman please speak into the microphone and read more slowly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- To be the commander, the commander of the Crisis Staff. Now, other than Gojko Klickovic up in Krupa, do you know of anyone else who called himself commander of the Crisis Staff in any municipality?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not offhand, no. I was just checking the original language to make sure it was the word that appears in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Look then at the next paragraph: "The commander appoints a member of the Crisis Staff as coordinator of relations with the municipal leadership of the SDA and the HDZ." In any of these Crisis Staffs which you say were created as a result of this instruction, was there a coordinator relations with SDA and HDZ that you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm certainly aware that there were negotiations that were carried out between the SDS and those parties in the municipalities, whether the person conducting negotiations had that title I don't know in any particular case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That was my question. Are you aware of any Crisis Staff where the commander appointed one of its members as coordinator of relations with the municipal leadership of the SDA and the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So I take it it has to be your position then that Crisis Staffs were created in accordance with this language of this document, but they ignored everything but creating a Crisis Staff. There were other parts of it they didn't implement at all. They didn't have commanders, they didn't have the right membership they didn't have coordinated relations with SDA and HDZ. They ignored everybody but the order to create a Crisis Staff. Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that. I wouldn't say that, that they ignored everything. The membership of the Crisis Staffs in so far as they have been able to determined in various cases and various ways in general include the category of people that is mentioned in paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you told us at the beginning of your testimony earlier today that what you really wanted to do here as a witness was look at the available evidence, look at all the documentation you had, and give the Court the conclusion that you draw from that that you think is the most sensible, logical conclusion. I suggest to you that this order, as you call it, contained in paragraph 3 sets out in detail what is to be done. And if that was not done, then it's virtually impossible to draw the conclusion that the Crisis Staffs that were created were created in accordance with these instructions, but these clearly weren't. So I think that's an improper conclusion to draw, don't you? Just being fair.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think I said that they were formed on the basis of these instructions, and I think that is clear for the reasons that I have stated. Again, if every detail of the order -- if we don't have evidence that every detail of the instructions, I'm sorry, was carried out in every place, that's certainly not surprising.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm not asking --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it undermines the conclusion that the SDS ordered the creation of Crisis Staffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm not asking about every detail. I'm asking about any detail. I'm not saying that 5 per cent of this wasn't done, therefore it didn't happen. I'm saying 95 per cent of this wasn't done. The only thing that you can tell us that was done was that this document existed, and a Crisis Staff was formed. That's all. You can't go beyond --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the composition as laid out, generally laid out in the instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But it doesn't have that composition. You can't find one Crisis Staff that has the composition that this instruction talks about, can you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: With that exact composition, I can't think of one. But in general terms, that is the composition.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I just have --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is, that those categories of people are represented on the Crisis Staffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm not going to pursue this matter with you any further because I think we've covered it. I have one more question to ask you about the variant document. There's nothing at all in this document, is there, that makes reference, any reference whatsoever, to the formation of any regional Crisis Staffs or regional organisations?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, certainly isn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, I want to go to - and I'm going to get the term exactly right this time - your report called the Bosnian Serb leadership 1990 through 1992 dated 30 July 2002. And I want to go to page 66. At page 66, you're referring - if you look at page 103 - you're referring to Municipal Assemblies created, operating pursuant to the constitution of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina of 1990.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And in paragraph 104, you tells that the Municipal Assembly was the highest organ of authority in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you derive that from the constitution itself or do you derive that from some other source?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's just look at --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's logical. I just wonder where you found it. I agree with the statement, by the way.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would proceed from the constitution where assemblies are in general are described that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now this is the same constitution and the same amendments that the preamble of the ARK statute says it was created under, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I take it you would then take the same position that the ARK assembly was the highest organ of authority of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, that voluntary association of municipalities called the Autonomous Region of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, it purported to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So whether we're talking about a municipality or the Autonomous Region of Krajina or any other body, its authority would derive solely from the assembly, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Let me amend that. I think its authority would derive from the constitution or whatever, which specifies the assembly as being the highest organ of authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Constitution through the assembly.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think we can agree with that. I want you to look now at P168. Now, P168 is one of those documents, sir, that there are several versions of.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But the version makes no difference with regard to the question I'm getting ready to ask you. This is the document that allegedly created the what in the document is called the war staff the Autonomous Region of Krajina with Radislav Brdjanin as president. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Bearing in mind the discussion we've just had, notice that this document was issued by Nikola Erceg, president of the executive council of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I take it you'll agree with me that there's nothing in the ARK statute that authorises the creation of a Crisis Staff in the Autonomous Region of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you want to look?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there was any authority to do that, it would have been -- in the terms of that body, it would have been the assembly that would have had authority to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You say --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is certainly no explicit reference to Crisis Staffs in the statute, but there are a lot of powers discussed in the statute. And as we were discussing, the supreme authority is the assembly, so one would expect if anyone -- one could perhaps expect that if anyone was going to do this, it would be the assembly. On the other hand, we've just been discussing, all the other Crisis Staffs that we have documentation about were, in fact, created by the SDS. So I would rather have expected someone of that nature to be signing a document of this type.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you have any evidence, documentary or otherwise, that would indicate that the ARK Assembly gave Erceg authority to create a Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prior to this, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Since we stopped at quarter to 11.00, we keep to the hour and a half, we should stop in about six, seven minutes' time. I just wanted to draw your attention to that, Mr. Ackerman, unless there is consensus that we go on until 12.30, and then we reconvene 25 minutes later. But I think it would make more sense that we stop in seven minutes' time. So you have enough material to carry on for the next seven minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to refer you now to Bosnian Serb leadership 1990/1992 addendum regarding instructions to the Autonomous Region of Krajina, page 18, your report.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir, paragraph 26. In paragraph 26, you are discussing generally provisions which authorised emergency bodies in certain emergency situations. And you say this: "The underlying features of the system of emergency rule at the federal, republican, provincial, and municipal levels were similar. If an assemble, the highest organ of authority in the municipality, is unable to meet, an emergency body was to exercise authority within the assembly's competence - and I want to emphasise that - within the assembly's competence until such time as the assembly was once again able to meet and approve the actions of the emergency body." That's a totally accurate statement, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it's accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The emergency body could only act as a sort of substitute for the assembly and only within the competence of the assembly.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the general principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And once the assembly could meet again, it then had to report and had to have whatever it did approved by the assembly, and then the emergency body would disappear?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that there could be a situation in which the assembly might be able to gather as a one-time thing and approve what has been done, and then the situation might be such that they knew they wouldn't be able to get together again for a while so the emergency body might continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Of course, of course that could happen. But the basic concept was that once the assembly could begin meeting again, then the emergency body could dissolve?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. And the concept of a Crisis Staff, a war staff, a war presidency was simply a way to implement this emergency body proposition that we have been talking about?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, "simply a way," it's a way to implement that idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: But of course, it's being implemented through -- in a manner that is not prescribed by the legal provisions we are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And we're referring to the ARK statute?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the paragraph of the report we were discussing previously, we were referring to the constitution of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and related documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But we know that there was an emergency body created to exercise authority within the ARK assembly's competence until such time as that assembly was able to meet again. That emergency body was called the ARK war staff or the ARK Crisis Staff, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, I'd like you --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This would be a good time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So we'll have a 25-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. The witness, where is he? When I say we are going to have a 25-minute break, never take me seriously because you are going to have a 25-minute break. I never have one minute break. I end up in my Chambers with problems from here and problems from there. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, we've located the exhibit of the speech.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What word did Mr. Karadzic use?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Stepen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did he use the word stepen?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry. The Exhibit number is P2383.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Sutherland. Thank you. Can we proceed, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I've had Ms. Philpott pull that document. If you think it's necessary to show it to the witness, but I concede, Your Honour, that he said "stepen."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I mean, I haven't seen it, but I take your word for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that matches the word in the variant document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The next document I want to refer to is P285. Now, P285 is a document dated 17 July 1992. It is a meeting of the Assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina held on that date with 99 members of the assembly present. And Item 4 on the agenda is verification of the decisions and conclusions adopted by the Crisis Staff and war presidency of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, what it specifically refers to is the decisions and conclusions of that body. Right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If we then look over at Item 4, verification of decisions, conclusions adopted by the Crisis Staff and war presidency of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. Following a debate in which several assembly members took part, all decisions and conclusions adopted by the Crisis Staff and war presidency of the Autonomous Region of Krajina were verified. And then the next two paragraphs indicate that 98 people voted for that proposition, and one voted against it. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see the 98 voting in favour. Yes, next page, 1 member voted against.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. I take it you have no idea who it was that voted against?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want you to look now at P227. Now, this is some conclusions drawn by the Crisis Staff on 26 May 1992. And you'll see the part I'm interested there in paragraph 1. It says that "the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina has absolute support for its work since it is now the highest organ of authority in the Autonomous Region of Krajina as the Assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina cannot function due to objective and subjective circumstances."

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Page 29, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Something's wrong. I'm looking at P227. And it's actually conclusion number 17. That's where the problem is. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There we go.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Paragraph 1 under conclusions, do you see paragraph 1 there?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, that language sort of matches the things that we have been talking about before the break, that when the assembly can't meet, an emergency body of some kind can take its place. And what they're saying there is the assembly can't function due to objective and subjective circumstances, and therefore this body, the Crisis Staff, is taking its place.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And has -- the assembly, having been the highest organ of authority, is now replaced by the Crisis Staff, which is now the highest organ of authority.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And as you indicated in your report, it is exercising -- the Crisis Staff then is exercising authority that's within the competence of the assembly, same authority.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think in the report we indicated that under the legal system of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that that is the case in relation to the - and I can use the term now, I think - the sociopolitical communities within that republic. What's happening here is certainly analogous to that. I would only point out that the Autonomous Region of Krajina was not a sociopolitical community within the framework of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: So anything it is doing, irrespective of the fact that in its preambles and so forth, it may say it's basing itself on the constitution, is basically on its own authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But the proposition that you stated in your report transfers appropriately to this situation; in other words, the Crisis Staff, substituting for the assembly, certainly does not have authority that exceeds that of the assembly. It cannot have, it's functioning --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that model.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah, it's functioning under the ARK statute?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Deemed to be following that model.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And if we go back then to Exhibit P80 --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, if I may be allowed to supplement my answer to your question --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me go ahead and ask you the next question, and then if you have something you want to supplement, we can talk about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, can Mr. Treanor be allowed to finish his question -- his answer, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. You are right, Ms. Sutherland. Mr. Treanor, please go ahead --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just wanted to point out as Mr. Ackerman has been asking about the basis within the ARK statute for the powers of the assembly as those -- of those of the Crisis Staff as those being of the assembly, as we saw in the statute, the assembly did not have the authority to bind the municipalities by its decisions. They only became valid when the municipalities approved them. In this conclusion in the second paragraph of point 1, it says that the decisions of the Crisis Staff are binding for all the Crisis Staffs in the municipalities. So in this respect, the power of the Crisis Staff is going beyond what the assembly had -- the ARK assembly had assigned itself in its own statute.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The statute of the autonomous region which you now have before you, if you look at -- the part I want to draw your attention to is - let me find it - it's Article 38. Article 38 talks about the manner in which the statute may be amended. And it says that a proposal to engage in the procedure of amending the statute of the Autonomous Region of Krajina may be submitted by the assembly, the assemblies of the associated municipalities and the executive council. The proposal referred to in the preceding paragraph shall be communicated to the assemblies of the associated municipalities for their consideration and for the purpose of obtaining their opinions. And then after their opinions have been obtained or after a given deadline has expired, the assembly shall consider the draft enactment on amendments or additions to the statute and transmitted to the assemblies of the associated municipalities to obtain their approval. And finally having attained the approval of the associated municipalities, the assembly may then declare the amendments and additions to the statute adopted.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So that's the procedure that would have to be carried out to amend, for instance, Article 35 of the statute. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And to my knowledge, and tell me if you know of anything, to my knowledge, there is no ARK document where the Assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina amended Article 35, is there?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there is a document which -- in which the Crisis Staff does so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand that. But I didn't ask you that. I asked you if the assembly --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There may be a document, and the timing is escaping me at the moment. There may have been a subsequent decision similar to the one that you -- that we discussed earlier in which the assembly approves all the acts of the Crisis Staff. There may be a decision of that nature that encompasses the decision to amend the statute.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But we just looked at Article 38, amending the statute requires the approval of all of the associated municipalities. I'm suggesting to you that the Crisis Staff had no authority to amend the statute of ARK unless they complied with Article 38.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that would certainly be true. But what the procedure was before the issue of that decision, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But you don't know -- I mean, there's no indication whatsoever that the procedure outlined in Article 38 was followed, is there?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Apparently not. I think we would need among other things the records of the Crisis Staff meetings to determine what sort of process may have been followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, again, I'll remind you that the burden here is upon the Prosecution to prove the case beyond a reasonable doubt. Look again, then, at Article 35. That could be read with the Crisis Staff substituting for the assembly.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article 38? I'm sorry, is --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Article 35.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, 35 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Second paragraph. That could be read with the Crisis Staff substituting for the assembly, that the decisions and conclusions of the assembly shall become binding for the member municipalities once they have been approved by the assemblies of municipalities, or you could put in, you could substitute Crisis Staffs of municipalities for assemblies, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I don't have them with me today. I can perhaps let you look at them tomorrow. But maybe you're aware of them as you sit there, a decision or two from the Prijedor Municipality Crisis Staff that they were not going to follow decisions coming from the ARK Crisis Staff. Do you remember that decision?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes indeed. That's referred to in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The addendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to look now at Document P157. This is a document of 26 April 1992, and it's entitled "Excerpt from the instructions of the work of the Municipal Crisis Staffs of the Serbian people." That phrase would cause one to believe that there were more detailed instructions somewhere that this was excerpted from. Have you ever seen the more detailed instructions?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that there must have been something like that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one must certainly be led to believe that there was, or at least it was intended that there be.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This was issued by Branko Djeric who was the prime minister. And I think it might be useful before we go any further to discuss the organisation of the government just a little bit. There was the assembly, and I think you'll agree with me that the assembly was, as you have said, the highest organ of authority of the government of the Serbian Republic of -- of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. But then they had created this part called the government which was headed by a prime minister and included all of the deputies and so forth. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And this document was issued by what was called the government through its prime minister, Branko Djeric. Have I got that right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let's look at -- if you wanted to compare it, for instance, to the typical municipality or even the ARK situation, Djeric was occupying a position which might earlier have been called president of the executive council?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Paragraph 3: "The Crisis Staff coordinates the functions of authorities in order to ensure the defence of the territories, the safety of the population and property, the establishment of government and the organisation of all other areas of life and work. In so doing, the Crisis Staff provides the conditions for the municipal executive committee to exercise legal executive authority, run the economy, and other areas of life." Now, this paragraph clearly contemplates that when the assembly can't meet and the Crisis Staff is in existence, the executive committee, the municipal executive committee, will continue to function and exercise executive authority through that period, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it certainly seems to contemplate the possibility that it might be continuing to function, or more precisely attempt to function, but I think it would also cover the contingency where the executive committee wasn't able to function at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But the effort here seems to be to provide conditions where that municipal executive can function?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. And the reasons for it not functioning could be various. And the way of its functioning could be various.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Were you aware that the ARK executive committee actually did function and remain active throughout the life of the ARK Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Paragraph 4: "The command of the TO and police forces is under the exclusive authority of the professional staff; and therefore, any interference regarding the command of the TO and/or the use of the police forces must be prevented." In other words, the TO and police forces have their own chain of command, their own structure. And the Crisis Staff ought not to be interfering with them, and they ought to keep anyone else from doing so.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Paragraph 6: "The work of the Crisis Staff is based on constitutional and legal provisions and on decisions reached by the Assembly, the Presidency, and the Government of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina." We talked before we started referring to these paragraphs about the organisation of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Those are basically the three components of that government, the Assembly, the Presidency, and the Government. Right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So what it's referring there is all three components, that the Assembly is the highest organ, there's the Presidency, and the Government and the Crisis Staff operates pursuant to decisions reached by those bodies?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What this sets out is the chain of authority, the chain of authority runs from the Assembly, the Presidency, and the Government, down to the municipality and its Crisis Staffs. Right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not quite sure that those are links in a chain necessarily, especially given the situation at the time when this document was issued. If I can elucidate on that, at the end of April, indeed the second half of April and through the first half of May, the assembly was not meeting. The acting presidents were exercising emergency powers. And most decisions were being taken -- important decisions at the top were being taken within the framework of the National Security Council, which included the two acting presidents, the president of the assembly, the president of the government, and the president of the SDS. So as I say, the idea of a chain here may not be exactly appropriate. I think -- the main idea may be that you're asking is yes, the Crisis Staffs responded to the central authorities. And my point here was they were not hierarchically tiered, one upon another at this point in time, but rather they were all sitting in the same room and making decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Certainly, the prime minister made decisions and issued this excerpt on the 26th of April?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What paragraph 6 doesn't say may be as important as what it says. It doesn't say that the work of the Crisis Staff is based on decisions reached by any regional authority, does it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Paragraph 8 speaks of the relationship between the paragraph and the JNA. And just so we're clear, we're talking about a period of time, 26 April, before the VRS was created, aren't we?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, right. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What the excerpt says with regard to that relationship is that the Crisis Staff has the obligation to provide working and living conditions for the JNA, for the members of the JNA, to ensure a fair attitude toward JNA officers and soldiers, and to prevent them from being humiliated or insulted in any way. It certainly doesn't indicate that there is any relationship which would contemplate command of the JNA by a Crisis Staff, is there?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Right. And finally, I just want to refer very briefly to paragraph 14. It says: "The Crisis Staff shall convene and make decisions in the presence of all its members, take official minutes, issue written decisions, and submit weekly reports to the regional and state organisations of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina." In any of the research that you have done, did you find that this paragraph was followed by all the municipal Crisis Staffs? Have you found these weekly reports that were supposed to be submitted --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- From each of these staffs? Do you think this was a situation where the documents were simply lost or this document was simply ignored, or do you know?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me finish answering the previous question. I also certainly couldn't say that every Crisis Staff met with all its members all the time, nor can I state that they always took official minutes. I have seen many minutes of meetings. We have seen many written decisions by those bodies. I haven't seen any weekly reports. I would suspect - I believe I pointed out at the beginning of my direct examination - that the records at our disposal are incomplete, and that the record that may have been created was itself quite likely incomplete. So yes, it may be that some of the Crisis Staffs did not do some of these things. And if they did them, maybe we don't know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: One thing that you alluded to just a few moments ago was that we're at the 26th of April now, and a lot of things were going on. One of those being a war. And so the assembly was not meeting, emergency organisations were trying to function. I think it would be fair to say that there was a great deal of chaos, even anarchy, throughout the country at this period of time. And whether or not decisions were followed and documents prepared and sent as ordered was a sometime thing, sometimes impossible, sometimes just ignored. There's a lot in that question. You're capable of taking it apart. I've seen you do it before.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I don't think I would exactly put it in those terms. There undoubtedly was a large degree of disorganisation, anarchy, failure to follow proper procedures, et cetera, et cetera. How large that degree was, I don't know. The thing that strikes me on the basis of only those documents we have at our disposal is the degree to which an attempt was made by the Bosnian Serb authorities to adhere to many of the various administrative niceties by formulating and publishing in Official Gazettes for a body, the Autonomous Region of Krajina, which didn't even legally exist under the law of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the keeping of minutes on various levels, and that sort of thing, the amount of documentation that's available is indeed impressive, given the wartime situation you're describing. It was undoubtedly not a very complete record that was being kept. And as I alluded before, even in peacetime, it was difficult sometimes for Radovan Karadzic as the president of the party, to get people to do what he wanted them to do and to report that and that sort of thing. So yes, there was failure to observe some of the niceties. But the degree to which that may have prevailed is almost ipso facto impossible to say on the written record since what we have reflects the organised part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: One of the things I've never seen, and I've tried to pay attention, is any evidence, documentary, testamentary, any kind of evidence that there was any kind of punishment mechanism that was carried out for failure to implement any of these conclusions and decisions and so forth that we have been talking about. We go back earlier to what we are talking about, the variant A/B thing, where you Karadzic ordered Crisis Staffs to be put together. We talk about this one which talks about the weekly reports. There are any number of conclusions, decisions, orders, whatever you want to call them that were issued by various bodies including the ARK Crisis Staff. But I do not know of one instance of punishment for failure to carry out, do you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the prewar period, there is certainly evidence that Karadzic had people removed from party positions for failing to do what he thought they should do. There were changes made in the municipal leadership of the SDS, in certain locations. The Crisis Staffs, there were -- I think there were some changes there. What the basis for such a decision might have been in any particular instance, I don't know. And that there was any sort of organised tribunal or forum that monitored what people were doing and brought them to task, I'm certainly not aware there was anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I can see those changes, but I suggest those were more based on personalities than failure to carry out specific orders, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that each case was a case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We kind of digressed from where we were going, and I want to go -- I want to try to get back into the chronology that we were working through, which means we have to go back to early 1992. And I'd like you to look now at Exhibit P19. Now, this is a document which is dated 9 January of 1992. Right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you are referring the witness to P19 --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's the wrong document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Absolutely the wrong document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Because the Document P19 --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah, I agree that's some other document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- Is dated 13 September 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Here's what we're going have to do -- now, I don't know what exhibit number this is because it apparently got mismarked.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: First look at the very top so we can see the designations on it. The P19 up there was I think put there when it was delivered to us from the Office of the Prosecutor. That's probably how I got confused about it being Exhibit P19. The second page, though, will show you the date that I was referring to. And that's 9 January 1992. Right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And to put this document in context, this document is issued two days before the decision of the Badinter Commission saying that they were not going to approve independence for Bosnia-Herzegovina yet. Right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The first paragraph is a kind of a preamble and suggests that this action is being taken, this proclamation of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, is being taken on the basis of the plebiscite of the 9th and 10th of November of 1991. And then in the second paragraph, it's proclaimed that the republic shall remain within the Yugoslav federal state as its federal unit. True?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, I don't recall without looking, so Ms. Philpott -- the usher could help me. Is there anything on there that I have marked with a yellow pen? I don't think so. I think mostly what I was interested in is bringing the date of this document to your attention, so you can bring it back to me now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm through with it. You can bring it back. At some point I need to figure out whether this is an exhibit in the case, Your Honour, and if so, designate it properly or admit it as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Gustin, there was the ERN number --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've just passed Ms. Gustin the ERN number, and she is checking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can perhaps identify the document whether it has already been tendered or whether it needs to be tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: While we're doing that, I'm going to have you look at Document DB-163.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That's Prosecution Exhibit P2471.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That was P2471, for the record, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So what I originally referred to as P19 is P2471, so the record will be clear about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I don't know what exhibit P19 is at the moment. But I thought you just referred to DB-163, and I was just advising that that's Prosecution Exhibit P2471.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: DB-163 is?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, and for the record, DB-162 is Prosecution Exhibit 2475.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Incidentally with reference to DB-162, the exhibit is divided into two parts, the first part being a speech by someone who I would like to know who it is, and the second part being the minutes of the 14th session of the meeting of the Assembly of the Serbian people of BH. Who was -- whose speech is it in the beginning of --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's Krajisnik, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. If you look at the end, after all the names have been named, he says: "And myself, Momcilo Krajisnik." That's how I concluded who it was that made the speech. I had the same problem as you did, Your Honour, yesterday when I was trying to figure out who it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So it's DB-163 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I take it you now have that document. This document is 27 January -- well, actually that's not true. This document is 9 January 1992, the same date as the other document we were just referring to, and still a document preceding the decision of the Badinter Commission saying no to independence.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That first page that's kind of a preamble --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: May we go ahead, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you look at that first page, one, two, three, the fourth paragraph down, it says: "The destruction and dissolution of the Yugoslav federation would cause irreparable damage to all Yugoslav peoples." That was fairly prescient, wasn't it, considering all the irreparable damage that has been done to Yugoslavia --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, I'm not sure why they would say would.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: They are talking about a period of time before independence was granted.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say it already had.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I was being too subtle about it. But the point is this: The issue that was going on, that was live at this point, was whether or not Bosnia-Herzegovina was going to be declared an independent state. And you'll recall Izetbegovic saying at one point that he realised that going forward with that might mean war, but he thought that was the appropriate alternative if that's what it had to be. And I think what's being said here is that everybody knows there's going to be a war if this independence business goes forward. And it's going to cause irreparable damage to Yugoslav peoples. This is another effort to avoid that, to create a Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina and avoid having a war about this. Isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this document is certainly -- contains an expression of the will of the Serbian people to remain within Yugoslavia, there's no doubt about that. The state had largely dissolved already.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The political coalition --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: But they definitely did want to keep Bosnia what remained in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: "The political coalition of the Muslim and Croatian ethnic communities in Bosnia and Herzegovina is joining to the secessionists in their efforts to break up Yugoslavia. In its bid to effect Bosnia and Herzegovina's secession from Yugoslavia, this coalition is grossly and flagrantly ignoring the sovereign rights of the Serbian people, trying to strip them of their status as a constituent nation, and impose their interests and decisions on them." Now, that's pretty much exactly what had happened in the assembly in Sarajevo on the 14th and 15th when it was real clear that the Muslims and Croats were not going to consider the wishes of the Serbian people. And in spite of their opposition, they were going to hold a rump session of that parliament and vote for independence. So they were flagrantly ignoring the sovereign rights of the Serbian people in doing that, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not a lawyer, let alone a constitutional lawyer, and I really couldn't speak to that issue. All I could say is this is a fair statement of the view of the Bosnian Serb leadership of that situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which leaves you exactly where you started from, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I suspect so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If we look then past the preamble over to page 3 of the document, the declaration proclaims this Republic of the Serbian People of Bosnia and Herzegovina as a part of the federal state of Yugoslavia and one of its federal units. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. If you look at this document as a whole, look at all of this language, it's really an expression of a fire of the Serbian people to remain within a federal Yugoslavia in accordance with the results of the plebiscite of the Serbian people, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Two days later, January 11th, we know what happened with the Badinter Commission. That's -- we've already looked at that, I think. It's DB-161, I believe. I don't think we need to look at it again. After that decision on January 11th by the Badinter Commission, I want to just go back for a minute to October of 1991 and set the stage from that point with regard to what happened next. We will recall that in October of 1991 at the parliament, speeches of Izetbegovic and Karadzic, speeches that have become famous, I think, that were actually became part of the record here in greater detail this morning, those speeches were made. And they had a tone of finality to them, Karadzic saying if you go forward with this, the Muslim people may not survive, or something to that nature. It was that kind of rhetoric that was going on at the time, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In general terms, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think what I'd like to do, Your Honour, is leave it at that place and pick it up from there in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Only five minutes left in any case. Mr. Treanor, we need to stop here. We will continue tomorrow. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anything else before we adjourn?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't think I have anything, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. We stand adjourned until tomorrow morning at 9.00 in this same courtroom. Thank you.
